entries.content: I've held a 40% allocation to intermediate bond funds since 2015 and it's been my rock. Through every market wobble, that allocation provided the ballast I needed. The beauty of intermediate bonds is their predictable income stream and low correlation to equities. I rebalance annually and otherwise don't touch it—set and forget has worked beautifully for portfolio stability.

Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes. A bond fund with 5-year duration will lose approximately 5% in value for every 1% rise in interest rates. Intermediate bond funds typically have durations between 4-7 years.

Reviewed historical volatility of my intermediate bond position. Standard deviation remained under 4% annually during my holding period, compared to 15%+ for equities. This consistent low-volatility profile is why I treat this allocation as my stability anchor. The income generation covers most of the fund's expense ratio, making it essentially a low-cost hedge against equity drawdowns.

Intermediate bond funds gained popularity among conservative investors because they offered meaningful yield advantages over money markets while maintaining relatively modest price fluctuations. Their sweet spot in the yield curve historically provided attractive risk-adjusted returns. Many financial planners built model portfolios around a core intermediate bond holding precisely because clients could count on that portion of their portfolio to behave predictably quarter after quarter.

Bond fund total returns depend on two components: income (coupon payments) and price changes. When prevailing interest rates move, existing bonds reprice to reflect new yield expectations. The magnitude of price adjustment depends on the fund's duration profile and how far rates have moved from when the bonds were purchased.
